subject: dbms
title: Unit 1 — Smart Urban System ER Modeling Practice

items.q:
**Smart Parking System.** The city manages **Parking Lots** (lot ID, location, total capacity, operator). Each lot contains multiple **Parking Slots** (slot number, slot type — two-wheeler/four-wheeler/EV, status), where **slot numbers are only unique within a lot, not city-wide**. **Vehicles** (license plate, type, owner name) reserve a slot for a time window, generating a **Booking** (booking ID, start time, end time, amount paid, payment status). A vehicle may have many bookings across lots and times, but **a slot can have only one active booking at a time** — though many historically. Add a **Payment** entity linked **1:1** with Booking, and consider an EV-charging attribute/subtype for EV slots.

Draw the ER diagram with entities, attributes, keys and cardinalities.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: a weak entity.**

*"Slot numbers are only unique within a lot"* is the giveaway — **Parking Slot is a weak entity** of Parking Lot.
- **Double rectangle** for `Parking_Slot`, **double diamond** for the identifying relationship `CONTAINS`, **dashed underline** on `Slot_number` (the discriminator), and a **double line** for total participation.
- **Primary key = {Lot_ID, Slot_number}.**

**Parking Lot** — strong entity, PK `Lot_ID`, attributes location, total capacity, operator.
**Vehicle** — strong entity, PK `License_plate`.

**Booking** is the association between Vehicle and Slot and carries its own attributes, so model it as an **associative entity** (or an M:N relationship with descriptive attributes start time, end time, amount paid, payment status).
- Vehicle : Booking = **1:N** · Slot : Booking = **1:N** (many *historical* bookings).

**Trap:** *"only one active booking at a time"* is a **temporal business rule**, not a cardinality. A plain ER diagram **cannot express it** — state it as an assumption or a CHECK constraint rather than drawing it as 1:1.

**Payment** — 1:1 with Booking, so the FK may sit on either side; prefer the side with **total participation**.

**EV charging** — either an optional attribute on Slot, or a **subtype** of Slot in an EER generalisation.

items.q: **Public Bus Transit Network.** **Buses** (bus ID, capacity, fuel type) run on **Routes** (route ID, route name, total distance). Each route passes through an **ordered list of Stops** (stop ID, name, location) — model this as an associative entity **Route_Stop** carrying a sequence number, since the **same stop can belong to multiple routes and the order matters**. A **Trip** is a specific bus running a specific route on a specific date/time slot (trip ID, departure time, arrival time), so Trip is **uniquely identified by Bus + Route + Date/Time** — consider whether it needs a surrogate key or a composite one. **Passengers** can leave **Feedback** (rating, comments, timestamp) tied to one specific Trip.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: an associative entity carrying order.**

**Route_Stop** exists because Route : Stop is **M:N** *and* the relationship has an attribute — `Sequence_number`. An M:N relationship with descriptive attributes **must** become its own relation.
- `ROUTE_STOP(`**`Route_ID`**`, `**`Stop_ID`**`, Sequence_number)`, PK = **{Route_ID, Stop_ID}**.

**Trip** — the question asks you to choose:
- **Composite key** `{Bus_ID, Route_ID, DateTime}` — faithful to the stated identity, but a **three-part key that every child must carry**.
- **Surrogate key** `Trip_ID` with a **UNIQUE constraint** on the triple — simpler foreign keys everywhere else.

**Either is defensible; say which and why.** The surrogate is usually preferred precisely because `Feedback` then references one column instead of three.

**Feedback** — Trip : Feedback = **1:N**; each feedback references exactly one Trip (total participation on the Feedback side).

**Passenger** — if a city-wide `Citizen` entity exists, Passenger is a **role** of Citizen rather than a separate entity.

items.q: **Waste Collection and Recycling.** **Households** (household ID, address, zone) are served by **Waste Collection Vehicles** (vehicle ID, type — recyclable/general/organic, capacity). A **Collection Schedule** (schedule ID, day of week, time slot, zone covered) assigns one or more vehicles to a zone — Schedule and Vehicle are **many-to-many via an associative entity Scheduled_Run**. Each household can log a **Missed Collection Complaint** (complaint ID, date reported, description, status) which must reference a specific Household **and a specific Scheduled_Run — not just a Schedule, since the same schedule repeats weekly**. Decide whether **Scheduled_Run should be a weak entity dependent on Schedule + Date**.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: distinguishing a recurring plan from one occurrence of it.**

`Schedule` is *"every Tuesday 9am, zone 4"* — a **rule**. `Scheduled_Run` is *"Tuesday 12 August, zone 4, vehicle V7"* — **one occurrence**. A complaint must point at the occurrence, or you cannot tell which week went wrong.

**Yes — model Scheduled_Run as a weak entity of Schedule.**
- Discriminator: **`Run_date`** (dashed underline).
- **PK = {Schedule_ID, Run_date}**, double rectangle, double diamond, total participation.

It simultaneously resolves the **M:N between Schedule and Vehicle**, so it carries `Vehicle_ID` as a foreign key too.

**Complaint** — references **both** Household and Scheduled_Run, so it has **two foreign keys**; with Scheduled_Run keyed on a pair, the complaint carries `{Schedule_ID, Run_date}` together.

**Trap:** a very common wrong answer links the complaint to `Schedule`. It compiles, but every complaint then becomes ambiguous across weeks — the exact failure the question is set up to expose.

items.q: **Smart Streetlight Energy Monitoring.** Each **Streetlight** (streetlight ID, location, installation date, pole number) can have **multiple Sensors installed over its lifetime** as they are replaced when faulty (sensor ID, model, install date, removal date) — **Sensor is a weak entity whose identity depends on Streetlight + install date, since sensor IDs might be reused across devices**. Each sensor logs periodic **Energy Readings** (timestamp, wattage, voltage, status flag), and a Reading's uniqueness is **Sensor + timestamp**. Add a **Maintenance_Action** entity (action ID, technician, date, action taken) triggered when a reading indicates a fault, linked to **both Sensor and Streetlight**.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: a chain of weak entities.**

This mirrors the AIRLINE `FLIGHT → FLIGHT_LEG → LEG_INSTANCE → SEAT` chain — the key **grows at each level**.

- **Streetlight** — strong, PK `Streetlight_ID`.
- **Sensor** — **weak** on Streetlight, discriminator **`Install_date`**, PK = **{Streetlight_ID, Install_date}**. (Sensor IDs being reusable is precisely why `Sensor_ID` alone cannot be the key.)
- **Energy_Reading** — **weak on Sensor**, discriminator **`Timestamp`**, PK = **{Streetlight_ID, Install_date, Timestamp}** — a **three-part** key inherited down the chain.

**Maintenance_Action** — linked to both Sensor and Streetlight. Note this is **partly redundant**: the Sensor key already contains `Streetlight_ID`. Either link only to Sensor and derive the streetlight, or justify the direct link (for actions on the pole itself, with no sensor involved) — **saying which, and why, is the mark**.

**Trap:** `Removal_date` is an ordinary attribute, **not** part of the key — a sensor is identified by when it was *installed*, not when it left.

items.q: **Public Water Supply Complaints.** **Residents** (resident ID, name, address) are connected via a **Water Meter** (meter ID, installation date, meter reading) tied to **exactly one property**. Residents raise complaints modeled through **generalization**: a supertype **Complaint** (complaint ID, date raised, status, resolution date) with two subtypes — **Water Quality Complaint** (contamination type, water sample result) and **Supply Interruption Complaint** (start time of outage, restored time, area affected). Both subtypes **inherit the link to one Meter and one Resident**. Add a **Technician** entity assigned to resolve complaints, with an assignment relationship carrying **assigned date and resolution notes**.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: generalization / specialization (EER).**

- **Complaint** is the **supertype**, holding the attributes common to both — complaint ID, date raised, status, resolution date — **plus the relationships to Meter and Resident**, since both subtypes inherit them.
- **Water_Quality_Complaint** and **Supply_Interruption_Complaint** are **subtypes**, each holding only its own attributes.
- Drawn with the **circle/triangle specialization symbol** and a subclass line from the supertype.

**State the two constraints explicitly** — this is where marks are won:
- **Disjoint (d) vs overlapping (o)** — a complaint is presumably one kind or the other, so **disjoint**.
- **Total vs partial** — if every complaint must be one of the two kinds, the specialization is **total** (double line).

**Key insight:** *"both subtypes inherit the link"* is the reason the relationships live on the **supertype**. Duplicating them onto each subtype is the common error.

**Technician** — M:N with Complaint, resolved by an associative entity carrying **assigned date** and **resolution notes** (descriptive attributes on the relationship, not on either entity).

items.q: **Emergency Services Dispatch.** Citizens report an **Emergency Incident** (incident ID, type — fire/medical/accident, location, timestamp, severity level). **Multiple Emergency Units** (unit ID, type — fire truck/ambulance/police, home station) can be dispatched to **one incident**, and **one unit can respond to many incidents** — a genuine many-to-many. Model this via an associative entity **Dispatch** (dispatch time, arrival time, role at scene, status). Add a **Station** entity that each unit is based out of, and consider whether Incident needs a resolution/closure sub-entity.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: an M:N relationship with descriptive attributes.**

**Incident : Unit is M:N**, and the relationship carries **dispatch time, arrival time, role at scene, status** — attributes that belong to **neither** entity alone. A unit does not have an arrival time; a *dispatch of that unit to that incident* does.

- `DISPATCH(`**`Incident_ID`**`, `**`Unit_ID`**`, Dispatch_time, Arrival_time, Role_at_scene, Status)`, PK = **{Incident_ID, Unit_ID}**.

**Trap on the key:** if the same unit can be dispatched to the same incident **twice** (returns after refuelling), the pair is no longer unique and `Dispatch_time` must join the key. **Note the assumption either way.**

**Station** — Station : Unit = **1:N**, so `Station_ID` becomes a foreign key on `Unit`.

**Closure sub-entity** — justified if outcome and casualty data is **optional** (not every incident has it) or **multivalued**. If it is exactly one optional record per incident, a **1:1 optional relationship** is cleaner than piling nullable columns onto Incident.

items.q: **Community Event Management.** The city hosts **Public Events** (event ID, name, type, date, start/end time) at specific **Venues** (venue ID, name, address, capacity). A Venue can host many events, but **no two events may overlap in the same time slot at the same venue**. Citizens **Register** for events via an associative entity **Registration** (registration ID, registration date, attendance status). Introduce **Volunteers** (volunteer ID, name, skill) assigned to specific events at specific venues through a **ternary relationship Volunteer_Assignment** (event, venue, volunteer, role, shift timing) — since a volunteer's role **can differ depending on which event/venue combination** they are working.
items.answer:
**The construct being tested: a genuine ternary relationship.**

**Volunteer_Assignment is ternary** — Event × Venue × Volunteer — and the justification is stated in the question: *the role can differ depending on which event/venue combination*.

This is the same argument as `proj_guide`: **the three-way fact is not the sum of its two-way projections.** Split into three binary relationships and you can record that Priya volunteers at Event A and works at Venue 1, but **not what her role is for that combination**.

- Drawn as **one diamond with three lines**; descriptive attributes **role** and **shift timing** hang off the diamond.
- Reduces to `VOLUNTEER_ASSIGNMENT(`**`Event_ID`**`, `**`Venue_ID`**`, `**`Volunteer_ID`**`, Role, Shift_timing)` — PK is the **combination of all three** foreign keys.

**Registration** — Citizen : Event M:N, resolved by the associative entity.

**The overlap rule** — *"no two events may overlap in the same time slot at the same venue"* is explicitly flagged as *a business rule to note even if not directly enforced in the diagram*. **ER cannot express temporal exclusion.** State it as an assumption; enforce it with a constraint or trigger. Saying so **is** the answer.

items.q: **School Zone Traffic Safety.** Each **School** (school ID, name, address) has a designated **Safety Zone** (zone ID, radius, speed limit) monitored by one or more **Traffic Cameras** (camera ID, location, install date). Cameras record **Violation Incidents** (violation ID, timestamp, violation type, evidence image) — a **weak entity dependent on Camera, since violation IDs might only be locally sequential per camera**. Each violation is tied to a **Vehicle** (license plate, owner name, type) — an **external entity not owned by the city system**. Add a **Fine** entity (fine ID, amount, payment status) generated from a Violation Incident, **1:1 or 1:many depending on repeat offenses**.
items.answer:
**Constructs being tested: a weak entity plus an external-entity judgement call.**

- **School : Safety_Zone** — 1:1 (*"a designated zone"*). Consider whether Zone is really a weak entity of School.
- **Safety_Zone : Camera** — 1:N.
- **Violation_Incident** — **weak on Camera**, discriminator `Violation_ID` (dashed underline), **PK = {Camera_ID, Violation_ID}**. The stated reason — IDs *locally sequential per camera* — is exactly the weak-entity test.

**Vehicle** — the question flags it as *external, not owned by the city system*. Two defensible answers, and **naming the trade-off is the mark**:
- model it as an ordinary entity within this system (simple, risks duplicating data other systems own); or
- reference a **shared Vehicle Registry** entity (correct, but introduces a cross-system dependency).

**Fine** — the question says *1:1 or 1:many depending on repeat offenses*. Argue it: **one violation generally produces one fine (1:1)**; a 1:N is only needed if a single violation can accrue **multiple separate fines** (e.g. a late-payment penalty as a second Fine row).

items.q: **Public Library Digital Membership.** Citizens can become **Library Members** (membership ID, join date, membership type, expiry date) — **consider whether Member is a role/subtype of Citizen or a separate entity linked 1:1**. The library has multiple **Branches** (branch ID, name, address), and each **Book** (ISBN, title, author, genre) exists as multiple physical **Copies** (copy ID, branch ID, condition, availability status) — **Copy is a weak entity dependent on both Book and Branch**. A **Borrow Record** (record ID, issue date, due date, return date, fine amount) links one Member to one specific Copy; a copy can be borrowed by only one member **at a time**, but over its lifetime links to many borrow records. Add a **Reservation** entity for members waiting on an unavailable copy/title.
items.answer:
**Constructs being tested: a weak entity with TWO owners, and a subtype-vs-entity judgement.**

**Copy is weak on both Book and Branch** — so its key inherits from **both**: **PK = {ISBN, Branch_ID, Copy_ID}**. This is the case students most often get wrong, because the usual example has a single owner.

**Member vs Citizen** — argue one:
- **Subtype of Citizen** — correct if a member *is* a citizen with extra attributes; avoids duplicating name and address.
- **Separate entity 1:1 with Citizen** — acceptable, and preferable if the library system cannot depend on the citizen registry.

**Borrow_Record** — Member : Copy over time is **M:N**, resolved by the record carrying issue date, due date, return date, fine amount.

**Trap — the same one as problem 1:** *"only one member at a time"* is a **temporal rule**, not a cardinality. The diagram shows M:N historically; the exclusivity is an assumption or a constraint (e.g. at most one row with `Return_date IS NULL` per copy).

**Reservation** — note the question says *"copy/title"*: a reservation on a **title** (any copy will do) is modelled against **Book**; a reservation on a **specific copy** against **Copy**. They are different relationships — pick one and say why.

items.q: **E-Governance Grievance Redressal.** Citizens submit **Grievances** (grievance ID, date filed, description, priority, status) against a specific **Government Department** (department ID, name) regarding a specific **Public Service** (service ID, name, category) — so **Grievance's identity/context depends on Citizen + Department + Service**. Each grievance is assigned to one **Officer** (officer ID, name, designation, department ID); an officer handles many grievances. If unresolved within a time limit, a grievance is **escalated to a higher-ranking officer** — model via a **recursive relationship on Officer (Reports_To)** and an **Escalation associative entity** (grievance ID, escalated date, from-officer, to-officer, reason) to **track the escalation trail over time rather than overwriting the original assignment**.
items.answer:
**Constructs being tested: a recursive relationship plus history-preserving design.**

**Reports_To is recursive on Officer** — the same entity set at both ends, so **role names are mandatory**: `Supervisor` (1) and `Subordinate` (N). Without them the pair *(O12, O05)* is meaningless. Reduces to a foreign key `Supervisor_officer_ID` inside `OFFICER` referencing `OFFICER(Officer_ID)` — a **self-referencing** foreign key, nullable for the top of the hierarchy.

**Grievance context** — related to Citizen, Department and Service. Decide and justify: either a **ternary relationship**, or a Grievance entity with its **own surrogate key** plus three foreign keys. The surrogate is usually better here because Escalation must reference the grievance, and a three-part key would propagate.

**Escalation as an associative entity is the heart of the question.** The stated reason — *track the trail over time rather than overwriting the original assignment* — is a general design principle:

> **When the question says "track over time", you need a new entity, not an updated attribute.**

Overwriting `Assigned_officer` destroys history. A separate `ESCALATION(Grievance_ID, Escalated_date, From_officer, To_officer, Reason)` keeps the **full audit trail**, with PK = **{Grievance_ID, Escalated_date}** since a grievance may escalate more than once.

Note `From_officer` and `To_officer` are **two foreign keys to the same entity** — the same pattern as the two AIRPORT references in FLIGHT_LEG.
